items.prompt: What total-cost expression compares a preprocessing strategy across q queries?

options.text: Preprocessing cost P(n) plus q times per-query cost Q(n).
Only Q(n).
Only P(n).
P(n)·q·Q(n).

feedback.reason: The full workload is P(n) + qQ(n).

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Preprocessing runs once, contributing P(n). The query routine runs q times, contributing q·Q(n), so sequential work totals P(n) + qQ(n). If the data changes, add update maintenance U(n) per update; if results are emitted or an index is stored, account for those resources separately rather than hiding them in query time.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Write a lifecycle formula before comparing strategies: build + updates + repeated queries + mandatory output. Multiply only phases that actually repeat.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_only: Q(n) describes one query and omits both its q repetitions and the preprocessing that makes it possible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.preprocess_only: P(n) stops after construction even though the requested workload also executes q queries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.product_all: Build and query phases execute sequentially, so P(n) is added once rather than multiplied by every query.

items.prompt: For one membership query on an unsorted array, why can sorting first be worse than a direct scan?

options.text: O(n log n) sorting plus O(log n) query exceeds one O(n) scan asymptotically.
Binary search is never correct.
A scan is O(1).
Library sorting has no cost.

feedback.reason: Fast query time can be overwhelmed by a one-time preprocessing cost when q is small.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

For one query, a direct scan costs O(n). Sorting then searching costs O(n log n) + O(log n), whose sorting term dominates. Binary search is correct after a legal sort, but its one fast lookup cannot repay the larger construction cost. Reuse across enough later queries can reverse this comparison.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not optimize the isolated query while ignoring how many times it runs. For q = 1, compare the entire one-shot workloads.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_wrong: Binary search is correct on legally sorted data; the objection here is total cost, not search correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_constant: A worst-case membership scan may inspect all n positions, so its time grows linearly with input size.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_free: A library call still performs O(n log n) comparison work and must be charged to this one-query workload.

items.prompt: When do prefix sums become attractive for range-sum queries on a static array?

options.text: When O(n) preprocessing can be shared across enough O(1) queries.
For every single query regardless of n.
When arbitrary updates occur after every query and the prefix array is never repaired.
Only when each query outputs the full array.

feedback.reason: Prefix sums trade one linear build for constant-time query evaluation.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Building prefix sums scans n values once and stores cumulative totals. Each later range sum uses two prefix entries, so total work is O(n + q) instead of scanning each requested range. Reuse makes the build attractive when q or total queried range length is large, but an unrepaired data update makes later answers stale.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Prefix sums assume an additive range query and a validity lifecycle. State whether the array is static or include maintenance after updates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_query_always: One short range can be scanned for less work and memory than constructing a prefix array over all n values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.updates_frequent: Without repair, an update invalidates every later cumulative total that crosses its position and makes answers incorrect.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_large: Prefix sums accelerate additive aggregate evaluation; the amount of output is not what creates their reuse benefit.

items.prompt: A hash set is built for repeated membership queries. Which cost is easy to omit?

options.text: O(n) build work and O(n) expected storage, in addition to expected O(1) queries.
The number of queries never matters.
Every membership query returns n values.
A hash set always requires sorting first.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing can reduce query time by spending time and memory up front.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Building the set examines n inputs and allocates up to one entry per distinct value, giving expected O(n) construction and O(n) additional storage. Each of q lookups is then expected O(1), for expected total time O(n + q). Reporting only the lookup bound hides both the paid build and the memory that enables it.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Fast lookup is purchased with representation state. Always report construction and storage alongside the expected per-query benefit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_count_none: The build is recovered only through reuse, so q directly changes whether the index is worthwhile.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_n: A membership query normally emits one boolean; the O(n) resource is the stored index, not each result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting: Hash insertion does not require sorted input, so sorting would be an unrelated extra preprocessing phase.

items.prompt: What happens to a precomputed index when the underlying data changes?

options.text: It may need incremental maintenance or rebuilding before future queries are correct.
Preprocessing remains correct automatically.
Updates always make queries faster.
Only output size changes.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing assumptions include data mutability.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A precomputed structure represents a particular state of the source data. An insertion, deletion or value change can invalidate affected entries, so correctness requires either incremental maintenance with an explicit update cost or rebuilding before subsequent queries. Continuing to query stale state is not a faster degraded mode; it answers a different dataset.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Attach an invalidation rule to every index: which source changes affect it, how validity is restored, and what queries may run meanwhile.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.never_matters: An index derived from old values can disagree with the current dataset and return incorrect results after a change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_faster: Updates usually add repair or rebuild work; they do not guarantee any improvement to later query complexity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_only: The change affects the internal representation's correctness even when the shape of each query result stays the same.

items.prompt: Which distinction matters between offline and online queries?

options.text: Offline processing may reorder or batch known queries, while online processing must answer before future queries are known.
There is no algorithmic difference.
Online means outputs must be sorted.
Offline preprocessing is free.

feedback.reason: The availability of future queries changes legal preprocessing and batching strategies.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Offline processing receives the complete query set before answers are required, so it may reorder work, sort queries by a key or batch shared computation while restoring required output order. Online processing must answer each arrival without knowing future requests, ruling out strategies that depend on that knowledge. Both models still pay their actual time and memory costs.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: State when information becomes available and when an answer is due. 'Offline' permits future-query knowledge; it does not make preprocessing free.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_always: Knowing all queries can enable legal batching or reordering that an immediate-response online system cannot perform.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.online_sort_output: Online describes information arrival and response deadlines, not whether returned values happen to be sorted.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.offline_no_cost: Offline algorithms still execute preprocessing, store state and answer requests; only their information model differs.

items.prompt: Why can sorting as preprocessing be illegal even when it improves query time?

options.text: The original order or original indices may be part of the required result contract.
Sorting is illegal whenever it is O(n log n).
Sorting always removes duplicates.
Sorting is semantically illegal only when q = 1.

feedback.reason: A preprocessing transformation must preserve all required information or carry provenance.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Sorting preserves values and multiplicities but changes positions. If the contract asks for original indices, stable input order or mutation-free behavior, an in-place sorted representation alone has destroyed required provenance. A legal strategy must sort a copy, carry original indices or choose another structure; faster query time cannot compensate for changing result semantics.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Check semantic legality before cost. Record which information a transformation changes and how the required output reconstructs it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_slow_only: O(n log n) may be affordable; illegality arises only when sorting violates a required data or output contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates: Ordinary sorting rearranges equal values but does not automatically remove their occurrences from the collection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_query: The number of queries changes amortization, while preservation of order and indices remains a semantic requirement for every q.

items.prompt: How should a break-even query count be derived?

options.text: Write total-cost expressions for both strategies and solve where one becomes smaller.
Use the word many without a formula.
Compare only per-query terms.
Choose the strategy whose query variable has the shorter name.

feedback.reason: A break-even point follows from P1 + qQ1 versus P2 + qQ2.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Write totals T1 = P1(n) + qQ1(n) and T2 = P2(n) + qQ2(n), then solve the inequality T2 < T1 for q. When Q1 > Q2, the symbolic threshold is q > (P2 - P1)/(Q1 - Q2). This is only a time break-even; memory limits, update maintenance and constants can still reject the nominal winner.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Replace vague words such as 'many' with an inequality tied to n and the two complete workload formulas.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.guess_many: Without both formulas, 'many' provides no threshold and cannot adapt when n or query costs change.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_build: The break-even question exists precisely because the indexed strategy must recover an upfront construction cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: Identifier spelling changes neither preprocessing work nor the number and cost of queries.

items.prompt: Which costs belong in a preprocessing-versus-query comparison? Select all that apply.

options.text: One-time build or sort cost.
Per-query cost multiplied by q.
Additional index or table storage.
Variable and function names.

feedback.reason: A complete comparison covers total time and storage.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Construction contributes a one-time term, per-query work is multiplied by q, and the retained index contributes additional memory. These are independent resources and none can be inferred from a fast lookup bound alone. When the workload mutates data or emits large results, add maintenance and output terms to the same lifecycle model.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept `build`, `per_query` and `memory`; reject names because only executed work and retained state enter the resource model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Renaming a function or variable does not change construction, query executions, storage, updates or output volume.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.memory: A faster strategy may exceed memory limits.

items.prompt: Which workload properties make preprocessing more attractive? Select all that apply.

options.text: Many queries reuse the same data.
The underlying data changes rarely or not at all.
The per-query improvement is substantial.
One tiny query with no future reuse.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing pays off through reuse and stability.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A large q reuses the one-time build many times, static data keeps the derived state valid, and a large gap between direct and indexed query cost repays construction sooner. One tiny query provides no reuse and commonly lets the upfront phase dominate. These properties work together rather than making preprocessing universally good.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Preprocessing is most attractive when state is reusable, remains valid and saves substantial work per reuse.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_tiny_query: With no future reuse, the full build may cost more than directly answering the one small request.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.large_query_saving: Each query recovers more of the initial cost.

items.prompt: Which facts can make an index unattractive despite fast queries? Select all that apply.

options.text: The index exceeds available memory.
Maintaining correctness after updates is expensive.
Too few queries occur to recover build cost.
The index answers queries quickly.

feedback.reason: Query speed is only one part of a data-structure tradeoff.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

An index is infeasible if it cannot fit memory, unattractive if frequent updates make maintenance dominate, and wasteful if q is too small to recover construction. Fast queries are the intended benefit and must be weighed against those costs rather than counted as a disadvantage.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Evaluate the complete state lifecycle: allocate, build, maintain, query and release. A strong result in one phase cannot erase failure in another.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_fast: Reducing query time is the reason to consider the index and does not itself make the index unattractive.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.frequent_updates: Update cost becomes part of the workload.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.small_q: The amortized benefit is too small.

items.prompt: Which distinctions should be explicit in a repeated-query model? Select all that apply.

options.text: Static data versus data with updates.
Online arrival versus all queries known in advance.
One query versus many queries.
Whether loops are named outer and inner.

feedback.reason: The same asymptotic query primitive can lead to different total strategies under different workload contracts.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Static versus dynamic determines whether derived state stays valid; offline versus online determines whether future requests may be reordered or batched; one versus many determines whether construction is reused. The same O(1) or O(log n) query primitive can therefore belong to very different legal and economical strategies.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Put workload assumptions beside the complexity claim. Without them, a reader cannot tell whether preprocessing is legal, current or amortized over enough requests.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loop_names: Calling loops `outer` and `inner` conveys no facts about mutability, query arrival or reuse count.

items.prompt: Arrange the comparison of a direct strategy and a preprocessed strategy.

elements.text: Write the direct total cost for q queries.
Write build cost plus q times indexed query cost.
Choose the strategy that satisfies the full workload with margin.

feedback.reason: A query-only comparison is incomplete.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Both candidates need complete time expressions before they can be compared. The direct path repeats its work q times; the indexed path adds construction once and repeats the cheaper query. Memory and update validity then constrain the symbolic winner, and only the full model supports a choice.

items: Write the direct strategy's total cost across q queries.
Write preprocessing cost plus q times the indexed query cost.
Add storage, update-maintenance and semantic constraints.
Choose a legal strategy that fits the complete workload with margin.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not choose after comparing per-query terms alone. That comparison omits the very construction cost the later reuse must recover.

items.prompt: Arrange the prefix-sum workflow for a static array.

elements.text: Build the prefix array in O(n).
Answer it with a constant number of prefix lookups and subtraction.
Reuse the same prefix array for remaining queries.

feedback.reason: The one-time build is recovered through repeated constant-time queries.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The prefix array must exist before any constant-time range formula can use it. Each query then supplies its boundaries, two cumulative values are combined, and the same valid prefix state is reused. The sequence assumes the underlying array stays static; an update requires a maintenance step before reuse.

items: Build cumulative prefix values in O(n).
Receive a range [l, r] under the declared indexing convention.
Answer with the corresponding prefix difference in O(1).
Reuse the unchanged prefix array for the remaining queries.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: If the source array changes between steps, stop treating the stored prefixes as valid. Fast subtraction from stale state is an incorrect answer.

items.prompt: Arrange the review of a data structure under updates and queries.

elements.text: Derive the cost of each operation type.
Verify the maintained structure remains semantically correct after every update.

feedback.reason: Dynamic workloads need more than preprocessing and query terms.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

First count how many times each lifecycle operation occurs, then derive each operation's cost under the chosen representation. Multiplication by u and q yields the total-work formula. The final validity check is essential: an update routine with low cost is irrelevant if it fails to restore the invariant required by later queries.

items: Count construction, updates u and queries q in the workload.
Derive build, one-update and one-query costs.
Combine them as build + u·update + q·query.
Verify that every update restores the representation invariant before the next query.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Complexity and correctness share the same update contract. Never accept a total-time formula for a structure that may be stale when queried.

items.prompt: An unsorted array of n values receives q membership queries. Strategy A scans in O(n) per query. Strategy B sorts once in O(n log n) and uses O(log n) binary search per query. Select both total-time expressions.

strategy_b: O(n log n + q log n)
O(n log n + q log n)

strategy_b.sort_plus_queries: O(n log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: The direct scan repeats n work q times.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Strategy A may inspect n elements for each of q membership requests, so its total is O(qn). Strategy B performs one O(n log n) sort and then q binary searches at O(log n) each, giving O(n log n + q log n). The second expression is legal only if sorting preserves the required semantics or provenance.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: The formulas describe total time, not a universal winner. Substitute n and q, then check mutation, original-index requirements and whether sorting occurs in place.

items.prompt: A static array of n values is preprocessed into prefix sums, then q range-sum queries are answered. Select total time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: Each query is O(1), and the prefix array is not part of the returned output.

feedback.reason: The build scans n values and each of q queries uses constant work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Construction reads n values once, contributing O(n). Each range query performs a constant number of prefix lookups and arithmetic operations, so q queries contribute O(q); total time is O(n + q). The reusable prefix array stores n cumulative values, giving O(n) auxiliary space while the source remains static.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not report O(1) as total time: it applies to one query after the O(n)-time, O(n)-space structure has been built.

items.prompt: A hash set is built from n values and answers q membership queries in expected O(1) each. Select expected total time and auxiliary space.
constraints: Assume expected O(1) insertion and lookup and at most n distinct keys.

feedback.reason: Expected linear build plus expected constant-time queries gives O(n + q).

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Expected O(1) insertion across n input values gives expected O(n) construction, and q expected O(1) lookups add O(q), for expected total O(n + q). The set retains up to n distinct keys, so auxiliary space is O(n). These are expected bounds under the hash-table assumptions, not worst-case guarantees against adversarial collisions.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Name the expectation model and include stored keys. Saying only 'O(1) lookup' hides both construction and collision assumptions.

items.prompt: For n = 1,000 and q = 1, compare q linear scans with sorting once plus q binary searches using log2 n ≈ 10. Select the dominant operation estimates.
constraints: Ignore constants and treat one comparison as one unit.

feedback.reason: The formulas expose a break-even near ten queries under the simplified model.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

One linear scan costs about 1,000 dominant checks, so q scans cost 1,000q. Sorting costs about n log2 n = 10,000 comparisons and one binary search costs about 10, so the indexed total is 10,000 + 10q. Equality gives 1,000q = 10,000 + 10q, hence q ≈ 10.1; the simplified break-even is just above ten queries.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: This threshold is a dominant-operation estimate. Constants, in-place mutation, original-order requirements and storage can shift or invalidate the practical decision.

items.prompt: A mutable dataset of n values receives u updates. After each update, a full O(n) prefix structure is rebuilt, and q queries cost O(1) each. Select total time.
constraints: The initial build cost is included in the same asymptotic term.

feedback.reason: Each of u updates triggers linear rebuilding, while queries are constant-time.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The initial structure costs O(n) if it is built before the workload. Each of u updates triggers another full O(n) rebuild, contributing O(un), and q constant-time queries contribute O(q). Total time is therefore O(n + un + q), commonly simplified to O(un + q) when u ≥ 1. The repeated rebuild term exposes why a static prefix strategy may be poor for dynamic data.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: A query bound is valid only while the structure is current. Charging every required rebuild keeps correctness and cost in the same model.
